papers.title: Astragalus: Automatic Configuration Repair for Production Networks
papers.abstract: Network configurations are prone to errors, which can lead to catastrophic service outages. A tool that can achieve automatic configuration repair (ACR) is highly desired by operators. Existing tools for ACR follow a \textit{semantics-driven approach}: they model network semantics as a set of SMT constraints, and solve them for a location or fix of the error. Due to the complex semantics of networks, constructing and solving these constraints can be prohibitively expensive, making these tools neither general nor scalable. Inspired by automatic program repair (APR), we explore another direction, i.e., a \textit{syntax-driven approach}, which generates and validates syntactically-valid candidate updates without modeling program semantics, often drawing on existing code in the same repository. Following this direction, we propose Astragalus, a syntax-driven method for ACR. It uses multiple iterations of a "localize-fix-validate" pipeline to search for repairs, and proves quite effective on configurations of our production network. Specifically, we show that Astragalus can repair every incident in multiple sizes of a synthesized network, and 97.5% of the incidents on a real network, both with 15 types of errors injected, within an average time of 6.93 seconds. It has also provided valid repairs in under 6 minutes for 7 recent network incidents or undesired changes, in a real production network with O(1,000)~O(10,000) devices.
papers.title_text: Astragalus: Automatic Configuration Repair for Production Networks

papers.title: ATLAS: Expert-Guided Sustainable Satellite Backhaul for Off-Grid Wildlife Monitoring
papers.abstract: Remote wildlife monitoring increasingly depends on high-fidelity cameras and sensors deployed far from grid power and terrestrial networks. Low Earth orbit satellite links can provide connectivity in these settings, but their high power draw and variable bandwidth, combined with intermittent on-site solar harvesting, make continuous backhaul infeasible. Current systems therefore filter at the edge, with motion triggers that waste limited energy and bandwidth on environmental artifacts, or fixed vision models that cannot follow evolving expert objectives. We present \textsc{ATLAS}, an expert-guided edge-to-cloud system that treats satellite backhaul as a scarce resource for off-grid wildlife monitoring. \textsc{ATLAS} uses foundation models to compile natural-language expert intent into semantic scoring logic, combines semantic relevance with environmental and energy state, and uses a constrained reinforcement-learning scheduler to decide which clips to upload and when. As a representative case study, we deployed \textsc{ATLAS} for over six months across 18 off-grid salmon-monitoring river sites. \textsc{ATLAS} achieves a mean clip-selection accuracy of $87.4\%$, exceeding mean baseline accuracy by $26.4$ percentage points, while maintaining near-continuous operation through low-solar periods in which baselines incur 16.0\% downtime.
papers.title_text: ATLAS: Expert-Guided Sustainable Satellite Backhaul for Off-Grid Wildlife Monitoring

papers.title: AutoTailor: Automatic and Efficient Adaptive Model Deployment for Diverse Edge Devices
papers.abstract: On-device machine learning (ML) has become a fundamental component of emerging mobile applications. Adaptive model deployment delivers efficient inference for heterogeneous device capabilities and performance requirements through customizing neural architectures. SuperNet-based approaches offer a promising solution by generating numerous model variants from a pre-trained ML model. However, applying SuperNet in existing frameworks requires tedious model-aware development and time-consuming hardware-aware profiling, which limits their practical adoption. We present AutoTailor, the first framework to enable automated, end-to-end SuperNet-based adaptive model deployment for edge devices. Unlike manual SuperNet construction, AutoTailor employs a computation graph-guided compilation approach to automatically transform user-provided ML models into SuperNets. To support efficient specialization, AutoTailor incorporates learning-free latency and accuracy predictors, enabling low-cost yet accurate performance prediction. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that AutoTailor reduces the lines of code for SuperNet construction by 10.8--34.5$\times$, reduces predictor profiling time by 2.2--11.5$\times$, and achieves up to 15.60\% absolute accuracy improvement and 60.03\% latency reduction compared to state-of-the-art approaches across diverse models and devices. AutoTailor's source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/liu-mengyang/AutoTailor}.
papers.title_text: AutoTailor: Automatic and Efficient Adaptive Model Deployment for Diverse Edge Devices

papers.title: D-Pingmesh: Dynamic Probing and Fault Localization for Reconfigurable Datacenter Networks
papers.abstract: Pingmesh monitors datacenter networks through periodic pings between servers. In reconfigurable datacenter networks, topology engineering (TPE) and traffic engineering (TE) make uniform server-pair probing inefficient: a pinglist wastes budget retesting common paths while missing low-probability interfaces. Frequent control-plane updates further require rapid pinglist refresh, and cause path ambiguity at control-plane boundaries for fault localization. We present D-Pingmesh, a probing and fault-localization system co-designed with the TPE/TE control plane. Its control-plane-aware generator builds task-efficient pinglists by greedily admitting probes with high interface coverage under the current TPE/TE snapshot. An incremental replay-and-repair mechanism updates pinglists across reconfigurations rather than recomputing from scratch. At control-plane boundaries, a Rho-EM localizer jointly infers per-task old/new-path mixture weights and the fault set through EM-style iteration. We evaluate D-Pingmesh on an 8-pod reconfigurable topology under dynamic TPE/TE. At a 0.99 coverage target, D-Pingmesh uses 17.7x fewer tasks than Pingmesh and generates each pinglist about 5.1x faster than RD-Probe. In ns-3 simulation, boundary-aware localization improves micro F1 from 0.871 to 0.953 over the deTector PLL baseline. A testbed deployment demonstrates second-scale fault localization with low host overhead. These results demonstrate that D-Pingmesh is practical for reconfigurable datacenter networks with control-plane-aware monitoring.
papers.title_text: D-Pingmesh: Dynamic Probing and Fault Localization for Reconfigurable Datacenter Networks

papers.title: Energy-Aware Scheduling for Serverless LLM Serving on Shared GPUs
papers.abstract: As LLM inference becomes a major cloud workload, its growing energy footprint makes cluster-wide energy optimization increasingly important. Serverless LLM serving helps platforms absorb traffic volatility by elastically sharing GPU resources across models, but this sharing also makes energy optimization difficult. Multiple co-resident models run under one device-wide operating point, while their resource demands and latency slack change across execution phases and load conditions. As a result, minimizing energy requires coordinated scheduling across request placement, runtime resource adaptation, and workload consolidation. We present Festina, a profiling-guided, power-aware control plane to minimize cluster-wide energy for serverless LLM serving. Unlike common global-local schedulers that focus on throughput or tail latency, Festina makes energy-first decisions by jointly coordinating request placement, SM partitioning, and GPU operating points under TTFT/TBT SLOs. In our system, a lightweight global scheduler performs fast, SLO-safe, energy-aware placement using constant-time lookups from offline profiles and GPU state summaries. On each GPU, a phase-aware local scheduler continuously adapts task batching and compute resources to minimize power consumption. Festina further performs energy-aware workload consolidation to reduce GPUs' static power consumption via SLO-aware migration. Comparison with four SOTA LLM serving systems and one DVFS-augmented system demonstrates that Festina reduces energy consumption by up to 56% while maintaining parity in SLO attainment (within a 2% margin)

papers.title: FlexMARL: Graph-Driven Rollout-Training Co-Design for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Despite algorithm-level innovations for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), the underlying infrastructure for large-scale MARL remains underexplored. Existing training frameworks primarily optimize for single-agent scenarios and fail to capture the graph-structured nature of MARL. This fundamental mismatch leads to three MARL-specific challenges: topology-induced rollout skew, critical path synchronization barriers, and dynamic training demand. To bridge this gap, we propose FlexMARL, a graph-driven rollout-training co-designed framework for large-scale LLM-based MARL. FlexMARL introduces the multi-agent execution graph (MEG) and materializes the intermediate representation as the MEG Store, which provides decentralized multi-table storage and serves as the data hub for system components. Built around the MEG Store, the Rollout Engine develops dependency parallel sampling with hierarchical load balancing, which reduces inference latency and balances intra-agent/inter-agent loads. The Joint Orchestrator exploits an agent-level asynchronous pipeline to mitigate the critical path synchronization barriers while maintaining consistency. The Training Engine achieves on-demand resource allocation by collectively managing training processes for individual agents. The training states of different agents are swapped via location-agnostic communication APIs. Empirical results on a production cluster demonstrate that FlexMARL achieves up to 7.3x speedup and improves hardware utilization by up to 5.6x compared to existing frameworks.

papers.title: gKSM: GPU Memory Deduplication at Driver Layer for Serverless LLM Inference
papers.abstract: In serverless LLM inference, cloud providers commonly locate multiple instances on a single GPU to improve utilization. However, each instance independently maintains its model weights and runtime state, making duplicate GPU memory the primary bottleneck. Memory deduplication is a widely-used technique for eliminating duplicate data in CPU systems, but extending it to GPU memory faces fundamental challenges. Effective GPU memory deduplication must avoid redundant data movement between CPU and GPU while preserving write isolation for shared pages without native copy-on-write (COW) support. This paper presents gKSM, a transparent GPU memory deduplication framework for serverless LLM inference. gKSM addresses these challenges through CPU-GPU collaborative hash management that offloads hash computation to GPU kernels, zero-copy model weight deduplication that eliminates duplication before model weight transfer, and a cross-privilege page fault handler that combines a lightweight kernel hook and CUDA Virtual Memory Management (VMM) remapping in the user space. gKSM also designs a stable page scanning algorithm and a reuse-aware placement policy in cluster scale. Experiments show that gKSM reduces GPU memory usage by 59.8% while maintaining high throughput compared to ServerlessLLM. Under memory constrained workloads, gKSM improves aggregate throughput by 2.15X and supports five instances concurrently. In cluster level simulation, gKSM achieves a service rate of 99.97%, compared to 78.2% for SLInfer and 26.9% for ServerlessLLM.
papers.title_text: gKSM: GPU Memory Deduplication at Driver Layer for Serverless LLM Inference

papers.title: HybridQC: Hardware-Grounded Simulation of Tightly Integrated Hybrid Quantum-Classical Systems
papers.abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical performance depends on how quantum processors share classical compute, controllers, memory, and communication links. Circuit simulators and provider measurements expose kernel and job behavior, but leave topology-level questions about controller bottlenecks, quantum capacity, and mixed-workload contention unanswered. We present HybridQC, a discrete-event simulator for configurable hybrid compute units (HCUs). Users specify resource graphs containing classical compute, memory, controllers, quantum annealing (QA) and digital quantum computing (DQC) devices, and links. Jobs become dependent stages for preparation, quantum execution, transfers, reconstruction, and postprocessing. Finite capacities and selectable scheduling policies determine where stages wait and overlap. Service profiles use measurements from D-Wave Advantage 1 and Advantage 2 and IBM Kingston, Marrakesh, and Fez, separating physical quantum-processor occupancy from cloud wall time. Mean absolute percentage errors are 3.92%-8.04% for D-Wave access time and 5.26%-19.01% for IBM quantum seconds. Balanced 10x HCU scaling improves makespan by 2.19x-3.42x, while policy choice changes makespan by 1.80x for a mixed workload with 20 jobs per workload family. Scaling depends on which inputs grow: 100x data growth yields median runtime near 306 s, while 100x joint growth in circuits, shots, and depth reaches 4.806 x 10^7 s on the fixed HCU. HybridQC enables designers to study topology, scheduling, and workload growth before tightly integrated quantum-classical machines exist physically.
papers.title_text: HybridQC: Hardware-Grounded Simulation of Tightly Integrated Hybrid Quantum-Classical Systems

papers.title: HYPIC: Position-Independent Caching for Hybrid-Attention LLM Serving
papers.abstract: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agentic LLM serving, prompts are assembled from multiple independent segments into long contexts, making prefill dominate the computation cost. To reduce this cost, position-independent caching (PIC) admits KV reuse for non-contiguous segments across requests, while hybrid-attention models reduce computational complexity using linear attention. However, existing PIC methods break down on hybrid-attention models because their per-token KV-cache reuse primitives do not transfer to per-request recurrent states. In this work, we present HYPIC, the first system to accelerate hybrid-attention LLM serving with position-independent caching. For linear-attention layers, we identify the segment-cumulative transition operator as the missing algebraic primitive and cache it for each segment, enabling near-exact and constant-time state composition. For the remaining full-attention layers, we construct a small seam window to propagate hidden states through the linear-attention layers, so that cross-segment attention can be repaired by recomputation. Finally, HYPIC introduces segment parallelism, which parallelizes cache-miss prefill across instances, turning long cold requests into an accelerable workload. Evaluated across four hybrid-attention models and five workloads, HYPIC reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) by $3.25\times$ on average and improves QPS by $1.66\times$ over Prefix Cache, while preserving task quality with a $1.71$-point gap from Full Recompute.
papers.title_text: HYPIC: Position-Independent Caching for Hybrid-Attention LLM Serving

papers.title: InfiniLoRA: Disaggregated Multi-LoRA Serving for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: LoRA enables efficient customization of LLMs and is widely used in multi-tenant and multi-task serving. However, emerging model architectures such as MoE significantly increase LoRA memory cost, making existing coupled LoRA serving designs poorly scalable and prone to tail-latency inflation. We present InfiniLoRA, a disaggregated LoRA serving system that decouples LoRA execution from base-model inference. InfiniLoRA introduces a shared LoRA Server with parallelism-aware execution, SLO-driven provisioning, and critical-path optimizations, including GPU-initiated communication and hardware-specialized LoRA kernels. Experiments show that InfiniLoRA can achieve an average 3.05 × increase in serviceable request rate under strict latency SLOs, and improves the percentage of LoRA adapters satisfying the SLO requirement by 53.1%.

papers.title: Instrumentation Optimization for Practical Dynamic Race Detection
papers.abstract: Dynamic data race detectors are successful at flagging concurrency bugs, but their high runtime overhead limits adoption. This overhead stems primarily from pervasive instrumentation of memory accesses -- a significant fraction of which is for safe accesses. We address this inefficiency through a compiler-integrated approach that identifies safe accesses using static analysis and eliminates instrumentation for these. We strike a careful balance between analysis precision and cost, to ensure applicability to real-world applications. We show that our optimizations never cause ThreadSanitizer to miss races it would otherwise detect. We further observe that many checks are redundant: They only flag a race if a preceding check has already flagged an equivalent race for the same memory location. We show that, when reporting one representative per class is sufficient, even more instrumentation can be eliminated. Lastly, we introduce a dynamic technique that skips instrumentation when there is only one thread at runtime, even when this could not be determined statically. We integrate these static analyses and program transformations into the ThreadSanitizer race detector based on LLVM. Our experiments on a diverse suite of real-world applications, including Memcached, Redis, SQLite, MySQL, and Chromium, demonstrate that our optimizations reduce the number of instrumentation calls at runtime by up to 91% and yield application-level speedups of up to 1.91x, a geometric-mean Chromium speedup of 1.25x on Blink and 1.14x on Speedometer 3.0, and peak speedups reaching 2.28x on Memcached with two server threads. Our optimizations are in the process of being upstreamed into ThreadSanitizer.
papers.title_text: Instrumentation Optimization for Practical Dynamic Race Detection

papers.title: NosRacer: Dynamic Detection of Race Conditions in On-Device Network Operating Systems
papers.abstract: Commercial on-device network operating systems (NOSes) run the complex control planes of production routers and switches, where configuration update tasks are executed by multiple loosely coupled components through asynchronous message passing. Such executions are prone to race conditions: the same ordered input commands may produce different outcomes when messages are delivered in different orders. The race conditions are difficult to expose because they often manifest only as subtle, delayed malfunctions. Existing static analysis techniques lack scalability and precision for large-scale industrial NOSes, while dynamic ones incur substantial system-execution cost when attempting to cover the space of asynchronous message interleavings. To address the challenges above, we present NosRacer, a dynamic analysis framework for race condition detection in industrial-grade on-device NOSes. NosRacer uses a two-phase design. The concentration phase reduces analysis scope by leveraging the locality of configuration update tasks. Race condition detection is then limited to a small subset of involved components and crucial state variables, thereby reducing the detection cost. The perturbation phase proactively perturbs message asynchrony to increase the likelihood of executions with race-condition-exposing message interleavings. It keeps perturbation practical by grouping compatible perturbations for parallel execution and adaptively strengthening perturbations. We implement NosRacer in a commercial, actively developed NOS. NosRacer is integrated into the existing testing factory and used to detect race conditions in 5 key control-plane components. NosRacer achieves 66% precision and detects 21 race conditions confirmed by developers as severe bugs, while keeping the detection overhead below 10%.

papers.title: PrefixFlow: Training-Time KV Caching for Schedule-Level Prefix Reuse in LLM RL Training
papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL) post-training, one prompt fans out into $N$ trajectories, yet standard trainers replay the shared prefix's forward and backward pass $N$ times; in long-context retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and multimodal workloads, this repetition dominates training compute. Existing designs reuse the prefix within one computation graph (a packed sequence, fused kernel, or tree traversal); under the trainer's memory limits and parallelism, their compute savings do not reliably become shorter steps. We present PrefixFlow, which takes the prefix out of that graph and into the training schedule through a training-time KV cache: Phase A runs one prefix forward and caches its keys and values ($K/V$); Phase B trains suffixes as ordinary microbatches that read only $K/V$ and write back only their gradients ($gK/gV$); Phase C runs one delayed prefix backward on the accumulated $gK/gV$. Memory and parallelism then become manageable: dormant prefix activations are offloaded during Phase B to free high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for suffixes, and context, pipeline, and data parallelism each schedule the phases through a local rule while tensor and expert parallelism need no change, so saved compute becomes shorter steps under any microbatch split. On dense models, and on mixture-of-experts (MoE) models under Rollout Routing Replay, PrefixFlow matches full-sequence training within bfloat16 (BF16) tolerance. Against an identically configured baseline, it speeds up end-to-end verl RL training on a long-prefix RAG workload by $1.90\times$ ($6.1\times$ on the actor update). In controlled sweeps, actor-side speedup grows with prefix ratio and group size, reaching $4.4\times$ at an 83% prefix ratio, while suffix-dominated splits gain little; offloading dormant prefix activations lowers Phase-B peak HBM by up to 59% and extends trainable sequences by $1.66\times$.
papers.title_text: PrefixFlow: Training-Time KV Caching for Schedule-Level Prefix Reuse in LLM RL Training

papers.title: Requests of a Feather Must Flock Together: Batch Size vs. Prefix Homogeneity in LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Auto-regressive token generation in large language models is memory-bound because it requires "attending to" key and value tensors (KV cache) of all previous tokens. Prior work aims to improve the efficiency of this decode process by batching multiple requests together, and maximizing batch size subject to GPU memory constraints. The key observation of our work is that with prefix-sharing workloads, smaller, prefix-homogeneous batches - where all requests share a common prefix - can achieve higher decode throughput than larger, heterogeneous batches, due to better spatial and temporal locality during KV cache accesses. However, current prefix-aware schedulers maximize prefix reuse within a batch only to reduce KV cache memory footprint, but do not stop batch formation at smaller homogeneous batches that could have performed better. Further, we show that shared prefix detection in existing schedulers relies on radix-tree traversals, incurring substantial CPU overhead that is often comparable to GPU execution time. This paper presents Feather, a prefix-aware scheduler that uses reinforcement learning (RL) to learn the optimal tradeoff between batch size and prefix homogeneity. We also introduce Chunked Hash Tree (CHT), a lightweight data structure that enables fast prefix detection and efficient request selection for the RL scheduler, avoiding expensive tree traversals. We integrate Feather into vLLM and SGLang, and our evaluation shows that Feather achieves 2-10$\times$ higher end-to-end throughput as compared to existing schedulers by reducing the total number of KV cache accesses, while doing no worse than the status quo when there is insufficient prefix sharing.
papers.title_text: Requests of a Feather Must Flock Together: Batch Size vs. Prefix Homogeneity in LLM Inference

papers.title: Rocks, Pebbles and Sand: Modality-aware Scheduling for Multimodal Large Language Model Inference
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) power platforms like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, enabling rich interactions across text, images, and videos. Unlike text-only workloads, multimodal requests are inherently heterogeneous, differing by orders of magnitude in latency and memory footprint. Existing LLM serving systems, designed for homogeneous text workloads, struggle under this heterogeneity: large image and video requests monopolize GPU resources, causing severe head-of-line blocking and degrading the responsiveness of lightweight, latency-critical text queries. Recent multimodal serving systems mitigate this interference through disaggregation, isolating encoding and inference stages across GPUs. While effective at large scale, such designs introduce severe GPU underutilization in more practical, moderate-scale deployments. In response, we build RPS-Serve a modality-aware scheduling framework that leverages the extreme heterogeneity in multimodal workloads and introduces a simple abstraction: videos behave like rocks, images like pebbles, and text like sand. Then, it lets sand flow quickly through pebbles and rocks, maximizing GPU utilization while ensuring fast responsiveness for lightweight requests and controlled execution for heavier ones. To achieve this, RPS-Serve estimates the GPU admission cost of each request, classifies requests into rocks, pebbles, and sand using lightweight clustering, and applies priority-based scheduling with aging to balance performance across modalities. Evaluation across state-of-the-art MLLMs shows that RPS-Serve increases GPU utilization by 65% and reduces TTFT by up to 9.3x, on average across models, compared to disaggregation-based multi-modal systems.
papers.title_text: Rocks, Pebbles and Sand: Modality-aware Scheduling for Multimodal Large Language Model Inference

papers.title: Scaling LLM Agent Tool Access: The MCP Gateway
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on tool calling to complete tasks. Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes tool calling between LLM agents and tool providers. It reduces integration cost and drives rapid growth in tool scale. In production deployments, tool access becomes difficult to scale. On the tool provider side, legacy services are not directly callable through MCP; the rapid protocol development creates ongoing compatibility cost. On the agent side, the number of mounted tools is limited by the LLM context window and inference overhead; mounting a large tool set increases token usage and inference latency and can reduce task success rate. Moreover, for stateful MCP backends with multiple replicas, preserving session affinity increases client-side complexity. We present a cloud-scale MCP Gateway system. It breaks the direct-connect model on the data plane and offloads legacy service integration, consolidating incompatible MCP variants, access control, tool recommendation, and session-aware routing at the gateway. The conversion module supports 315 OpenAPI services in the cloud and integrates MCP transport variants. Session-aware routing decouples the scalability of the gateway layer and the MCP service layer. The hybrid retrieval engine sustains $\sim$98\% Top-15 recall; it scales agent tool access to 3{,}000+ tools with improved tool selection accuracy. We also share the lessons learned from deploying the gateway system in production.
papers.title_text: Scaling LLM Agent Tool Access: The MCP Gateway

papers.title: Schedules Are Solvable Symbols: Tuning-Free Compilation of Tile Programs on Dataflow Architectures
papers.abstract: Modern AI and HPC accelerators increasingly expose dataflow features: software-visible mechanisms for data movement and overlap, such as inter-core communication through the on-chip network and intra-core asynchronous pipelining. These features shift scheduling responsibility from hardware to the compiler, and because placement, movement, and synchronization become software-visible, they also make the performance of static schedules predictable. Yet high performance on such hardware still relies on vendor-engineered kernel libraries or profile-based auto-tuning, whose embedded expert knowledge transfers poorly across architectures and algorithms. We present Loom, a tuning-free symbolic compiler framework for tile-based SPMD programs on spatial dataflow architectures. The central idea is to treat tile-based SPMD compilation as a hardware-explicit static optimization problem. Loom enumerates discrete spatial-mapping and communication candidates while keeping value parameters, such as tiling factors and pipeline knobs, symbolic within each candidate. From an explicit hardware description, it derives symbolic legality constraints and latency expressions, formulates one CP-SAT problem per schedule candidate, and jointly solves inter-core dataflow, intra-core asynchronous scheduling, and block sizes at compile time. On two Tenstorrent generations, Wormhole and Blackhole, Loom matches or exceeds the vendor-optimized TTNN library on GEMM, Flash Attention, and Flash Decode, out of the box and without per-shape profiling or profile-based platform-specific schedule tuning. These results suggest that hardware-derived symbolic compilation provides a retargetable alternative to profiling-based tuning for spatial dataflow architectures while remaining interpretable by keeping optimization decisions traceable to source-level symbols.
papers.title_text: Schedules Are Solvable Symbols: Tuning-Free Compilation of Tile Programs on Dataflow Architectures

papers.title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.
papers.title_text: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs
